sources.title: Institute for Language and Folklore: the name Sverige
sources.note: FAQ on Sverige: Svearike, svear and götar living farther south; both important in formation of Sweden. Imported name interpreted from its Swedish footprint, not equated with Gothic kingdoms around the Mediterranean.

sources.title: UNESCO: Birka and Hovgården
sources.note: Outstanding Universal Value, synthesis: harbour, royal domain, waterways, trade 750 to 980, Ansgar 829 to 831, late tenth-century cessation with qualified explanation.

sources.title: Swedish History Museum: the Birka Girl and other children
sources.note: Grave Bj 463, five to six years old, uncertain biological sex, expensive brooch/beads/knife/needle case. Trading town crafts and possible toys. Avoid unsupported population mortality estimate and categorical explanation of Birka abandonment elsewhere on page.

sources.title: Swedish History Museum: surviving the winter
sources.note: Display 34. Bone skates at Birka, average 20 cm, many without attachment holes; two interpretations. General Viking-period shoe spikes and healed fractures; no diagnosis of individual fall.

sources.title: Swedish History Museum: food for the poor and the rich
sources.note: Display 43, archaeological food residue and faeces, cereals and bread. Museum-wide regional synthesis; no later Eddic luxury menu projected uniformly onto ninth-century Sweden.

sources.title: Swedish History Museum: a wooden spoon for the soup
sources.note: Display 39: utensils, vessel materials, coals and suspension chains, preservation of wood. General Viking-period household evidence.

sources.title: Swedish History Museum: grooming and hygiene
sources.note: Display 35: combs, ear picks, tweezers, washbasins and glass mirrors. No repetition of Ibn Fadlan quotation or transfer of his Volga observations to all Swedish households.

sources.title: Swedish National Heritage Board: Rök stone photograph and description
sources.note: Archive KMB_16001000190066_rbog00011a, Ög 136 / Rök 1:1. Ninth-century monument by Varin for deceased son Vämod. Indexed original description checked; no controversial narrative interpretation used.

sources.title: Swedish National Heritage Board: memorial runestones
sources.note: Opening chronology places large memorial wave from late tenth to early twelfth century and Rök earlier in ninth century. Only this comparison used.

sources.title: Swedish History Museum: Sigtuna silver coin, object 3001088
sources.note: Direct object text, circa 995, English model, ONLAF REX AN STUE, Godwine moneyer, Digeråkra hoard in Gotland. Short original Latin inscription excerpt ONLAF REX retained without modernizing ONLAF; translated King Olaf. Catalogue mistakenly calls both inscriptions obverse, so draft does not assign sides.

sources.title: Stockholm County Museum: Sigtuna
sources.note: Sections Sigtuna anlades på 900-talet and Den första stenkyrkan. Foundation in 970s per excavation synthesis, early street plan, coinage around 995, Christian community from start. Later stone churches not imported into tenth century.

proposedOverrides.summary: Early communities of southern and central Sweden, with trading centres and developing royal power.

batchIdentityNotes.finding: Two imported phases 800 to 900 and 900 to 1000 occupy southern/central Sweden, bbox 11.8639186 to 19.0423904 E and 56.0353010 to 60.6804160 N. Read Goths in this composite atlas label as Götar, explicitly a map-identity inference supported by geography and Isof distinction. Not an alias for Visigoths, Ostrogoths or modern Sweden. No claim of a continuously unified kingdom or exact ethnic frontier. All twelve passages focus on 800 to 1000 or clearly labelled broader Viking-period material evidence. Gotland hoard findspot is not a claim that the entire island fell under one king.
